The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W10-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W10-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W10-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`. All of these, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W10-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W10-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.

Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.
* stores the address book data i.e., all `Person` objects (which are contained in a `UniquePersonList` object), whether they are archived or not.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.

* shows only some of those objects at a time. The filtered list uses a `Predicate<Person>`: `PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE` (persons who are not archived, the normal person list and the list shown at start-up) or `PREDICATE_SHOW_ARCHIVED`. `Model#showingArchivesProperty()` tells the UI which of the two is in use. See [Archive feature](#archive-feature).
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.

* saves every person, including archived ones, in the same file. A person's `archived` flag is stored as an optional `"archived"` key, which defaults to `false` when it is missing, so data files saved before archiving existed still load.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.

The `contexts` command lists active persons' distinct contexts with person counts in the existing scrollable result display. `AddressBookParser` delegates to `ContextsCommandParser`, which rejects non-whitespace arguments with the usage message and a pointer to `find c/CONTEXT`. Command words remain case-insensitive. The command stays separate from `list`, as `archives` does; `list` continues to show active persons and ignore trailing arguments.

`ContextsCommand#execute()` reads `Model#getAddressBook().getPersonList()` rather than the filtered person list. It visits persons in their stored order, skips those that do not match `Model.PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE`, and aggregates the remaining context descriptions in a `TreeMap` using `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`. This groups equivalent names and sorts the output while retaining the spelling from the first active person. Archived persons cannot contribute counts, context names or spelling. `Context` already normalizes surrounding and repeated spaces, and each person's contexts form a set, so a person contributes at most one to each context's count. Separate persons with the same name are counted separately.

The command returns one line per context followed by a distinct-context summary. An empty address book gets the add-person hint; an address book containing only archived persons gets a separate no-active-contexts message with instructions to view and unarchive persons. It does not update the model or its filter, so the displayed person list, search predicate, Archives header and indices remain unchanged. Even in the archive view, the overview counts all active persons, rather than the displayed archived persons. Counts are recomputed on each execution, and no storage format change is required. Existing `LogicManager` save handling applies as it does for other commands.

`ContextsCommandTest` covers normalization, counts, alphabetical order, spelling from the first active person, empty and archived-only data, filtered lists, archive views and changes between executions. Parser tests cover command casing, whitespace and rejected arguments. `LogicManagerTest` verifies filtering, archive/unarchive transitions, preservation of the archive view, rejected input and counts after reloading saved persons.

An archived person is an ordinary `Person` whose `archived` flag is `true`. It stays in the same `AddressBook` and the same data file as every other person. What changes is which persons the user *sees*.
The user sees `ModelManager#filteredPersons`, a `FilteredList<Person>`. The list that is shown depends only on the predicate set on it, in the same way as for `find`:
| Command | Predicate set | What is shown |
| `find KEYWORDS` | `PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE.and(keyword predicate)` | matching persons who are not archived |

Because the shown list is the predicate, no separate "view mode" is stored. The window shows the **Archives** header by binding to `Model#showingArchivesProperty()`, which is true only while the predicate is `PREDICATE_SHOW_ARCHIVED`. After a `find`, the predicate is a combined one, so the header is hidden.
The new commands follow the pattern of `delete`:

* `ArchiveCommand` and `UnarchiveCommand` take an `Index` that refers to `Model#getFilteredPersonList()`, that is, to the list on screen. The command finds the person, checks the flag (`archive` refuses a person who is already archived and `unarchive` refuses a person who is not), and replaces the person with `Person#copyWithArchived(boolean)`, which returns a copy with only the flag changed (`Person` is immutable). `LogicManager` then saves the whole address book as after every command.

* `ViewArchivesCommand` only sets `PREDICATE_SHOW_ARCHIVED`. Unlike the other commands without parameters, `ViewArchivesCommandParser` rejects text after the command word, because `archives` is one letter away from `archive` and `archives 1` is most likely a mistyped `archive 1`.
`archive c/CONTEXT` and `unarchive c/CONTEXT` change every person who has the context, in one command. The classes involved are shown below.
![Classes used by the archive and unarchive commands](images/ArchiveCommandClassDiagram.png)

* Archiving and unarchiving are the same change with opposite values, so each way of choosing persons has one command class with an `archived` flag: `SetArchivedByIndexCommand` (the index form) and `SetArchivedByContextCommand` (the `c/` form). `ArchiveCommand` and `UnarchiveCommand` are thin subclasses of `SetArchivedByIndexCommand`. They only give the command word, the usage message and the flag, so the code and tests that refer to them did not change.

* One `ArchiveCommandParser` serves both command words. `AddressBookParser` creates it with `true` for `archive` and with `false` for `unarchive`. It first asks `ContextArgumentParser` whether the arguments are in the `c/` form. If there is no `c/`, it continues with the index as before. This is why the parser returns `Command` and not `ArchiveCommand`.

`ContextArgumentParser` rejects `c/` together with an index or with any other prefix (for example `archive c/CS2103T n/John`), and rejects a repeated `c/`. It recognises every prefix defined in `CliSyntax` (including `+c/`, `-c/`, `-p/` and `-e/`) by tokenizing with `ArgumentTokenizer`, as `AddCommandParser` and `EditCommandParser` do, so the same rule decides where a prefix starts in every command: a prefix only counts after a space. A prefix added to `CliSyntax` must also be added to `ContextArgumentParser`; a test fails if it is not.
The sequence diagram shows what happens when the user enters `archive c/CS2103T`.
`unarchive c/CS2103T` is the same, with the flag `false`, so the command calls `copyWithArchived(false)`.

**Why two command classes.** `SetArchivedByIndexCommand` and `SetArchivedByContextCommand` are separate because the two forms behave differently, not only because they read different input. The index form points at one person on screen, so it reads `Model#getFilteredPersonList()` and reports a person who is already in the target state as an error (that is useful feedback for a single person). The context form asks for a group, so it reads the whole address book, skips persons who are already in the target state, and fails only if no person changes. Both build the changed copy with `Person#copyWithArchived(boolean)`. The Javadoc of each class names the other.

The command reads `Model#getAddressBook()` and **not** `Model#getFilteredPersonList()`. A context command has no index, so nothing ties it to what is on screen, and an earlier `find` must not change which persons it affects. The persons to change are copied into a list before the loop, because `Model#setPerson` changes the list that they were read from. Only persons whose state really changes are counted, and if there are none the command fails with a message that names the context. The context is matched with `Context#equals`, so it is exact and ignores capitalisation.

Because `unarchive` checks the flag of the person it finds, `unarchive 1` while the normal list is shown cannot change the wrong person: that person is not archived, so the command is refused with a message that says to run `archives` first.
Other commands take the archive into account as follows:
* `Person#isSamePerson` ignores the flag, so an archived person still blocks a new person with the same phone number or email, and `unarchive` can never create a duplicate.
* `clear` removes only persons who are not archived, so it cannot wipe the archive by accident.
* `delete` is unchanged. It deletes whichever person is shown, so it deletes an archived person while the archives are shown.

`JsonAdaptedPerson` has an optional `archived` value. A missing or `null` value means `false`. It is read as a plain object and checked in `toModelType()`: only `true` or `false` is accepted, because Jackson alone would also turn values such as `5` into `true`. Any other value makes the data file invalid, which takes the normal path for an unreadable file (the file is renamed to a `.bak` file and the app starts empty).
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** one list with an `archived` flag per person.
* Pros: one data file and one save, so there is no half-finished move between two files; the duplicate check already covers archived persons; old data files load unchanged.
* Cons: every command that shows a list must choose a predicate, or archived persons would appear; the flag touches `Person` and `JsonAdaptedPerson`.
* **Alternative 2:** a second address book and a second data file for the archive.
* Pros: existing commands never see archived persons, so they cannot forget to filter them.

* Cons: archiving writes two files, so a crash between the two writes loses or duplicates a person; the duplicate check must look in both address books; the UI must switch between two lists; and there are two files that can become unreadable.
**Aspect: How the app knows that the archives are shown**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** use the predicate on the filtered list as the only state.
* Pros: nothing can disagree with it, and `find` already works this way.
* **Alternative 2:** store a separate view mode next to the predicate.
* Cons: two copies of the same fact that can drift apart.
The `find` command supports two search modes while preserving the existing keyword-search behaviour:
* An unprefixed command such as `find Alex CS2103T` uses `PersonContainsKeywordsPredicate`. A person matches when
any keyword occurs in the person's name or contexts.
* A structured command such as `find n/Alex c/CS2103T nt/project` uses `PersonMatchesCluesPredicate`. A person
matches only when every supplied clue matches its corresponding field.
`FindCommandParser` uses `ArgumentTokenizer#tokenizeWithRestOfLinePrefix`, with `nt/` as the rest-of-line prefix, to
select the search mode and read the clues. If none of the supported prefixes is recognised, it creates the existing
keyword predicate. If at least one is recognised, it creates the structured predicate. `n/`, `p/`, `e/`, `a/` and
`i/` may each appear at most once, while `c/` is repeatable. The non-note prefixes may appear in any order before
`nt/`. When present, `nt/` must come last: everything after its first occurrence becomes the note clue, including text
such as `c/o` or `n/a` that resembles another prefix.
Before constructing `PersonMatchesCluesPredicate`, the parser trims each clue, collapses repeated whitespace and
removes equivalent repeated context clues case-insensitively. Empty clues and unprefixed text before a recognised
structured clue are rejected without changing the current filtered list. The normalised values are collected in a
`PersonSearchClues` builder using field-named methods, avoiding ambiguous positional arguments for the similarly typed
`FindCommand` stores a `Predicate<Person>` rather than a concrete predicate type, allowing both search modes to share
the same command execution. In structured mode, `PersonMatchesCluesPredicate` checks each clue only against its
corresponding person field and combines all results using AND. Each individual context clue may match any one of the
person's contexts. A person with a missing optional field does not match a clue for that field. Comparisons are
case-insensitive partial matches, with repeated whitespace treated as one space.
This separation keeps the legacy name-and-context OR search unchanged without changing `FindCommand` execution.

The proposed undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedAddressBook`. It extends `AddressBook` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as an `addressBookStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedAddressBook#commit()` — Saves the current address book state in its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#undo()` — Restores the previous address book state from its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#redo()` — Restores a previously undone address book state from its history.
These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` and `Model#redoAddressBook()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedAddressBook` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single address book state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the 5th person in the address book. The `delete` command calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing the modified state of the address book after the `delete 5` command executes to be saved in the `addressBookStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.

Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new person. The `add` command also calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If a command fails its execution, it will not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, so the address book state will not be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which will shift the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial AddressBook state, then there are no previous AddressBook states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather
than attempting to perform the undo.

Similarly, how an undo operation goes through the `Model` component is shown below:

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `addressBookStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone AddressBook states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. Commands that do not modify the address book, such as `list`, will usually not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` or `Model#redoAddressBook()`. Thus, the `addressBookStateList` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear`, which calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `addressBookStateList`, all address book states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …​` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

* is a Computer Science (CS) student at university
* actively builds and maintains academic and professional networks through modules, project teams, hackathons, tech communities, internships and other collaborative activities
* accumulates persons across many overlapping academic and professional contexts
* often remembers the context in which they know someone, but not the person's exact details
* has a need to manage a significant number of persons
* prefers desktop apps over other types of applications
* is reasonably comfortable using CLI apps

**Value proposition**: Help CS students organise and retrieve people in their academic and professional network, especially when they remember the context in which they know someone but not the person's exact details. Each person is saved with one or more contexts (e.g. a module, project team, hackathon or internship), so users can find the right person by name or context, faster than with a typical mouse-driven contact app.

2.  System adds the person and shows the details of the new person

* **Capitalisation**: Whether the letters in a context name are uppercase or lowercase.
* **Person**: A saved record representing a specific person within the user's academic, professional, or social network.

* **Context**: A descriptive tag representing the shared environment, activity, or relationship (such as a school module, project team, CCA, internship, or event) that explains how or where the user knows a specific person.
* **Archived person**: A person that has been set aside with `archive`. It stays saved but is left out of the normal person list and out of `find` results, and it is shown only by `archives`.
* **Index**: A numerical value used to identify and select a specific person based on its position in the currently displayed person list.
* **Partial-match**: A name/context input can match to multiple persons in the local JSON.
* **Case-insensitive**: No distinctions between uppercase and lowercase inputs including commands, names and contexts.
* **Session**: A single continuous period of using UniContacts, starting when the application is opened and ending when it is closed.

UniContacts is a **desktop contact manager for CS students, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). Every person is saved with one or more *contexts* describing how you know them (such as a module, a hackathon or an internship), so you can find people by where you met them. If you type quickly, UniContacts can help you manage persons faster than traditional GUI applications.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for UniContacts.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar unicontacts.jar`.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `contexts` : Lists all active persons' contexts with the number of persons linked to each.
* `add n/John Doe c/CS2103T p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com` : Adds a person named `John Doe` to the address book.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd person shown in the current list.
* `clear` : Deletes all persons except archived ones.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.

* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user. Some parameters come after a prefix that says what they are, such as `n/` for a name. Others, such as `INDEX` in `delete INDEX`, have no prefix.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [p/PHONE]` can be used as `n/John Doe p/98765432` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[c/CONTEXT]…​` may be omitted, or written as `c/CS2103T` or `c/CS2103T c/NUS Hackers`.
* Parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE`, `p/PHONE n/NAME` is also acceptable.
The exception is `nt/NOTE` in `add`, `edit` and `find`, which must come last.
* Command words are case-insensitive, but prefixes must be in lowercase.
For example, `add`, `ADD` and `Add` all work, but `N/John Doe` is not read as `n/John Doe`.
* Commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list` and `exit`, ignore anything typed after them.

For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. The exceptions are [`clear`](#clearing-all-non-archived-persons-clear), [`contexts`](#viewing-all-contexts-contexts) and [`archives`](#viewing-archived-persons-archives), which reject anything typed after them, so that a mistyped `clear 1` does not delete everything.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.

* To give more than one context, repeat `c/`, one context each. Every other prefix can be given only once.
* Spaces before and after each value are ignored.
* `nt/NOTE` must be the last parameter. Everything after `nt/` is the note, so text such as `c/o`, `n/a` or `p/t` inside a note is saved as part of the note.
* `add n/Alex Tan c/CS2103T` adds `Alex Tan` with just a name and one context.
* `add n/Priya Nair c/Hack&Roll 2026 c/NUS Hackers p/91234567 e/priya@u.nus.edu` adds `Priya Nair` with two contexts, a phone number and an email.
* `add n/Jean-Luc O'Brien c/Google internship e/jl.obrien@gmail.com` adds `Jean-Luc O'Brien` with an email but no phone number.
* `add e/mei@u.nus.edu c/CS2101 n/Lim Mei` adds `Lim Mei`, showing that parameters can be in any order.

`n/NAME` | Starts with a letter. Only English letters, spaces, hyphens `-`, apostrophes `'` and periods `.`. At most 100 characters. | `Alex Tan`, `Jean-Luc O'Brien`, `Lim J.H.` | `Alex123`, `Raj s/o Kumar`, `@alex`
`c/CONTEXT` | Starts with a letter or digit. Only English letters, digits, spaces and `&` `-` `.` `'` `#`. At most 50 characters. | `CS2103T`, `Hack&Roll 2026`, `Tut #3` | `CS2103T/T09`, `(orbital)`
`p/PHONE` | An optional `+`, then 3 to 15 digits. No spaces, hyphens or brackets. | `91234567`, `+6591234567` | `9123-4567`, `+65 9123 4567`, `12`
`e/EMAIL` | Of the form `local-part@domain`, at most 254 characters. See the email rules below. | `e0123456@u.nus.edu`, `alex.tan+work@gmail.com` | `alex@`, `.alex@gmail.com`, `alex..tan@gmail.com`
`a/ALIAS` | Alternative name; follows the same character and 100-character rules as `n/NAME`. | `Alex`, `Jean-Luc` | `Alex123`, empty `a/`
`i/INTRODUCER` | Plain name of the person who introduced this person; follows the same rules as `n/NAME`. It does not need to be another saved person. | `Ben Lee` | `Ben123`, empty `i/`

`nt/NOTE` | Short, single-line note of at most 300 characters. No line breaks or control characters. Must be the last parameter; the rest of the line is the note, so it can contain text such as `c/o` or `n/a`. | `Met at Hack&Roll`, `Lives c/o his aunt` | Empty `nt/`, a note over 300 characters
`/` is not allowed in names, so enter a name such as `Raj s/o Kumar` as `Raj s o Kumar` or `Raj son of Kumar`.
* The local part (before the `@`) may contain letters, digits and `+` `_` `.` `-`, but cannot start or end with a symbol, or have two symbols in a row.

* The domain (after the `@`) is one or more parts separated by periods, such as `u.nus.edu`. Each part may contain letters, digits and hyphens, but cannot start or end with a hyphen. The last part must be at least 2 characters long.
* Names, contexts and emails keep the capitalisation you typed.

* Several spaces in a row inside a context are saved as one space. For example, if you type `NUS`, three spaces, then `Hackers`, the context is saved as `NUS Hackers`. The 50-character limit is checked after this, so extra spaces never make a context too long.
* Names are saved exactly as typed, including several spaces in a row.
* Aliases and introducer names have surrounding spaces removed and repeated spaces inside collapsed to one. Notes have surrounding spaces removed.

* Contexts that differ only in capitalisation or repeated spaces count as the same context. If you give the same context twice, such as `c/CS2103T c/cs2103t`, the person gets it once, spelt as you first typed it.

UniContacts automatically saves data after every command. You do not need to save manually.

If a command cannot be saved, for example because the data file or the `data` folder is read-only, UniContacts shows an error message. The change stays in the current session but is not in the data file until a later command that changes something is saved successfully. If you close UniContacts before then, the change is lost. Commands that change nothing, such as `list` and `find`, do not need to save.

Each save is written to a temporary file first and then moved over `data/addressbook.json`. If UniContacts is closed or crashes in the middle of a save, your previous data file is left as it was instead of being half-written.

UniContacts data is saved automatically as a JSON file `data/addressbook.json`, in the folder you start UniContacts from (normally the folder that contains the JAR file). Advanced users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.
Each person is stored like this:
* `name` and at least one entry in `contexts` are required.
* `phone`, `email`, `alias`, `introducer` and `note` are optional. You can leave them out, as for Roy above, or set them to `null`.
* Each context is a plain piece of text, such as `"CS2103T"`, and must follow the same rules as a context entered in the `add` command.

* `archived` is optional. `true` means the person is archived (see [`archive`](#archiving-a-person-archive)), as for Roy above. `false`, `null`, or leaving it out, means the person is not archived, so data files saved by earlier versions still work.

* `archived` must be `true` or `false`, without quotes. Any other value, such as `"yes"` or `5`, makes the data file unreadable (see [If the data file cannot be read](#if-the-data-file-cannot-be-read)).
* Two persons cannot have the same phone number or the same email, whether they are archived or not.

Edit the data file only while UniContacts is closed, and only if you are confident that you can update it correctly. Certain edits can cause UniContacts to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range).
#### If the data file cannot be read

If UniContacts cannot read the data file when it starts (for example, a person has no context or has an invalid phone number or email, two persons share a phone number or email, the file is not valid JSON, or the file was saved by an older version that used addresses and tags), it:
1. renames the file to `addressbook.json.<UTC time>.bak` in the same `data` folder, for example `addressbook.json.20261015T101723Z.bak`, so that your data is not overwritten; and
2. starts with an empty address book. A new `data/addressbook.json` is created by the first command that changes something, such as `add`.
2. Open the `.bak` file in a text editor and fix the problem. The reason is written in the log file `unicontacts.log.0`, which is in the folder you started UniContacts from.

3. If there is a new `addressbook.json` (it exists if you ran a command that changes something, such as `add`, after the failed start), rename it to `addressbook-new.json` so that it is not overwritten. Then rename the fixed `.bak` file to `addressbook.json`.
4. Start UniContacts again. Any persons you added after the failed start are still in `addressbook-new.json`; add them again if you need them.

If UniContacts cannot rename the file, for example because the `data` folder is read-only, it still starts with an empty address book and leaves the file where it is. It renames the file to a `.bak` file just before its next save, so a save can never overwrite the unreadable file. The same applies when the `data` folder cannot be opened at all: UniContacts starts empty instead of with the sample data.

If UniContacts fails to read the data file more than once, each failure keeps its own `.bak` file, because the time is part of the name. If two failures happen in the same second, the later `.bak` file gets `-1` (then `-2`, and so on) before `.bak`, for example `addressbook.json.20261015T101723Z-1.bak`.
